# A Family's Sacrifice: The Weight of Service and the Policy That Shields the Last Son

*How one American family's losses illuminate a little-known military protection*

---

MARIETTA, Ohio — The Hendricks family kitchen still holds three coffee mugs that no one uses anymore. Margaret Hendricks can't bring herself to pack them away, though it's been four years since her second son died in Afghanistan.

"People ask why I keep them out," she said, her hands wrapped around a fourth mug—her own. "But when you've raised boys who wanted nothing more than to serve, you hold onto every small thing they touched."

The Hendricks family has become an unintended emblem of military sacrifice. Of their four sons, two were killed in combat operations overseas—Marcus, 24, in 2018, and Daniel, 22, in 2020. A third son, Thomas, served two tours before being medically discharged.

## The Sole Survivor Policy

It is their youngest, James, now 23, whose situation has drawn attention to a Department of Defense provision many Americans have never heard of: the Sole Survivor Policy.

Formally rooted in DoD Directive 1315.15 and shaped by decades of legislation, the policy allows service members who are the last surviving child in a family that has lost members to military service to be discharged or exempted from combat duty—if they choose.

"The intent has always been to prevent a family from losing all of its children to war," explained Dr. Eleanor Vance, a military policy historian at Georgetown University. "It gained public consciousness through popular culture, but its real history is one of quiet mercy in official policy."

The policy traces conceptual roots to World War II, when the loss of all five Sullivan brothers aboard the USS Juneau in 1942 shocked the nation and prompted changes in how the military handled family members serving together.

## An Impossible Choice

For James Hendricks, the policy presents a burden of a different kind.

"Everyone assumes I'll take the discharge," he said during an interview at his mother's home, his uniform pressed and formal despite the casual setting. "But my brothers didn't quit. How do I look at their graves and tell them I walked away?"

His mother sees it differently.

"I have buried two children," Margaret said, her voice steady but her eyes glistening. "I cannot bury a third. I won't survive it. And I need him to understand that staying isn't the only way to honor his brothers."

The tension is one that military chaplains and family counselors say is heartbreakingly common in these situations.

## The Emotional Toll

Chaplain Colonel Robert Whitmore, who has counseled Gold Star families for over two decades, said the emotional weight on surviving siblings is profound and often overlooked.

"We talk about survivor's guilt in combat," he said. "But there's a particular anguish for the young man or woman who lives while their brothers do not—and who may feel that policy is taking away their right to serve alongside their fallen family."

For the Hendricks family, grief has arrived in waves, each loss reopening the previous wound.

"When Marcus died, we thought that was the worst pain imaginable," Thomas Hendricks said. "Then we lost Daniel, and I realized grief doesn't have a bottom. It just keeps going."

The family has found some solace in a local Gold Star Mothers chapter, where Margaret now mentors newly bereaved parents.

"There's a sisterhood here that no one wants to join," she said. "But we hold each other up."

## A National Conversation

The Hendricks family's story has prompted renewed discussion about how the military supports families who have given so much.

Veterans advocacy groups point to gaps in mental health resources for surviving siblings and argue that the emotional dimensions of the sole survivor decision deserve more institutional support.

"The policy protects a life," said Maria Delgado of the National Military Family Association. "But we need to make sure we're also protecting the emotional wellbeing of the person making that choice, and their family."

The Department of Defense, in a statement, affirmed its commitment to supporting affected families: "We recognize the extraordinary sacrifices made by families like the Hendricks, and we remain dedicated to honoring their service while providing options that acknowledge their profound losses."

## The Path Forward

As for James, the decision remains unmade. He has requested time to consider his options—time the military has granted.

In the meantime, he visits his brothers' graves each week at the local cemetery, where two American flags snap in the wind above matching headstones.

"I talk to them," he admitted quietly. "I ask them what I should do. I haven't heard an answer yet."

Back in the kitchen, Margaret Hendricks continues her daily ritual, keeping the three unused mugs clean and ready, as though her sons might walk through the door at any moment.

"A mother's job is to protect her children," she said. "I couldn't protect Marcus. I couldn't protect Daniel. But maybe—maybe—I can still protect James. That's all I have left to give."

---

*The Sole Survivor Policy allows eligible service members to request discharge or exemption from hazardous duty. Families navigating loss can find support through the Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS) and other veteran service organizations.*

Jared Hubbard, the eldest of the three, was a Marine. In November 2004, he was killed by a roadside bomb in Ramadi, Iraq. His death sent shockwaves through the tight-knit Clovis community and devastated the family. Jared was remembered as a devoted son and brother, someone whose loss left an irreplaceable void.

## Grief Turned to Service

In the aftermath of Jared's death, his younger brothers Nathan and Jason made a profound decision. Rather than retreating from military service, they chose to enlist together in the Army, motivated in part by their brother's sacrifice and a desire to honor his memory. The brothers reportedly requested to serve in the same unit, invoking provisions that allowed family members to serve together.

## The Second Tragedy

In August 2007, tragedy struck the Hubbard family again. Nathan Hubbard was killed when the Black Hawk helicopter he was aboard crashed in northern Iraq, claiming the lives of all fourteen soldiers on board. In a devastating irony, Jason was also serving in Iraq at the time and was among those who helped recover his brother's remains.

## The Sole Survivor Policy

Following Nathan's death, Jason became subject to what is commonly known as the "Sole Survivor Policy"—a Department of Defense regulation designed to protect families who have already sustained the loss of members in military service. Under this policy, Jason was removed from the combat zone and returned home to his grieving family.

The policy, sometimes associated with the fictional dramatization in "Saving Private Ryan," exists precisely to prevent a family from losing all its children to war. For the Hubbards, it meant that Jason would survive—but at the cost of having buried two brothers.

## A Family Forever Changed

The Hubbard parents, Jeff and Peggy Hubbard, endured a grief that few can comprehend—the loss of two sons within the span of three years. Their story drew national attention, highlighting the deeply personal cost of war borne by ordinary American families.

## Legacy and Reflection

The Hubbard brothers' story raises enduring questions about sacrifice, service, and the human cost of war. It reminds us that behind statistics of casualties are real families, real communities, and real losses that echo for generations.

The Clovis community memorialized the brothers, ensuring their names and sacrifice would not be forgotten. Their story remains a testament to both the profound patriotism and the profound pain that military service can bring to a single family.
